title: All Teachers Need to Be Literacy Teachers
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler argues that integrating literacy with content instruction has to run in both directions: knowledge-building curricula bring science and social studies into the elementary literacy block, but secondary science, social studies and even math teachers must also take responsibility for helping students read their subject's texts. She focuses on syntax as an under-recognised barrier, citing research that unfamiliarity with complex sentence structure hinders comprehension more than vocabulary does as grades rise. Examples include word problems with convoluted phrasing, science texts that compress actions into noun phrases, and social studies textbooks dominated by the passive voice. She cites studies showing gains in science, social studies and even math from combined instruction. Her practical advice is to preview texts, teach vocabulary and guide students through hard sentences, and to teach sentence-level writing so students can recognise complex syntax in reading.
points: Literacy integration needs to flow both ways, so content-area teachers cannot treat reading comprehension as the English department's exclusive job.
Complex syntax, not only vocabulary, is a major and often neglected barrier, especially in older grades and in subject-area texts.
Even math suffers from linguistic complexity, since word problems demand tracking pronouns, the passive voice and multi-clause sentences.
Textbooks lean heavily on compressed constructions like nominalisations and the passive, so teachers cannot count on clearer texts and must prepare students for the real ones.
Previewing texts, teaching key vocabulary and having students write complex sentences within content they are learning is the most promising route to understanding difficult text.
quotes: We also need to make sure they can understand what they’re expected to read when learning about the Civil War or the human digestive system, where key vocabulary may be quite different.
researchers have found that lack of familiarity with complex syntax is a significantly greater barrier to reading comprehension than lack of vocabulary, especially as the grade levels go up.
One analysis of a fourth grade unit on fractions in a widely used math curriculum found that none of the lessons or assessments completely passed a check for linguistic clarity.
Rather than saying, for example, that “tectonic plates moved,” a textbook will refer to “the movement of tectonic plates.
The passive voice poses challenges for many students because it inverts typical English word order and obscures the person or thing that is doing the action.

Instead of simplifying the text or circumventing it with a PowerPoint, teachers need to help students learn and retain key vocabulary and act as guides through thickets of syntax.
ELA teachers will probably always take the lead on literacy instruction, but it’s far too complex—and too important—an area to be considered their exclusive province.
